plan.angle: Title: 'Do Semaglutide and Other GLP-1 Shots Affect Your Bones?' (no tirzepatide in the title). Open with the planned calm question. Body: 'A systematic review published on 23 Oct 2026 in Archives of Osteoporosis pooled 8 small randomized trials in adults with overweight or obesity (confirm the n from the abstract). Mostly exenatide and liraglutide, with only one semaglutide trial. Tirzepatide wasn't included. The certainty of evidence was very low, and the authors say it's too thin to tell whether these drugs help, spare or harm bone. Fracture trials are needed.' Then: 'Losing weight by any method can come with some bone loss.' Habits (general advice, not proven on the drug): muscle-strengthening at least 2 days a week, started gently, and a protein food at each meal unless your clinician has told you to limit protein. If you have osteoporosis or fracture risk, ask your clinician about bone health. One GI line (nausea is common). 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own.' 'Not personal advice' plus the prescriber line. No scare visuals.

plan.why: Runs the body-worry test the playbook asked for (macular degeneration: 104 on YouTube, 160 on Instagram). The review is brand new with low competition, and the topic suits women 50+ worried about menopause and bones. | fact-check: The review exists: Lai C-H et al., 'Skeletal effects of GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy in adults with overweight or obesity: a systematic review', Archives of Osteoporosis 2026; 21:148, published 23 Oct 2026, DOI 10.1007/s11657-026-01785-8. Per secondary coverage it included 8 RCTs (about 493 participants) covering exenatide, liraglutide, dulaglutide and semaglutide (1 trial). GRADE certainty was very low for every agent, and the conclusion was that the evidence is too sparse and too heterogeneous to establish skeletal effects. **Tirzepatide was not included.** That makes the working title, which names tirzepatide, misleading. The per-agent trial counts add up to 9 against 8 trials and the participant total needs checking, so confirm both against the Springer abstract before using them. Don't say 'no effect'; the review says the evidence can't tell. The habit advice and the clinician caveat are fine.

package.title: Do GLP-1 Meds Affect Your Bones? New Review #shorts
package.description:
A new review asks whether GLP-1 medicines affect bone density — here's what's actually known.

Quick answer: 8 small randomized trials, 493 adults with overweight or obesity (5 in type 2 diabetes); mostly older GLP-1 drugs, 1 semaglutide trial (lower spine bone density), no tirzepatide. Certainty is very low: too thin to say these drugs help, spare or harm bone. Nausea is common with GLP-1 medicines.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you. Don't switch, stop or change your current medicines on your own.

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26012544/

social.instagram_caption:
"Will this medicine weaken my bones?" If you're on a GLP-1 medicine and that question has crossed your mind, you're not overreacting.

Here's what a brand-new review actually found:
→ 8 small randomized trials, 493 adults with overweight or obesity (5 of the 8 trials were in type 2 diabetes)
→ Most tested older GLP-1 drugs (exenatide, liraglutide, dulaglutide) — only one used semaglutide, and none tested tirzepatide
→ Certainty of the evidence: very low
→ That one semaglutide trial saw lower spine bone density, but the authors say there isn't enough evidence to say these drugs help, spare or harm bone
→ We need fracture trials to really know

Separately, losing weight through diet alone has been linked to a small drop in hip bone density.

General habits, not proven on these drugs: muscle-strengthening at least two days a week, started gently, plus enough protein, unless your clinician limits it. If you have osteoporosis or fracture risk, ask your clinician about bones.

Nausea is common with GLP-1 medicines.

factcheck.summary: I checked all four sources. Each exists and says what the script claims. Lai, Li, Wu and Wu published "Skeletal effects of GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy in adults with overweight or obesity: a systematic review" in Archives of Osteoporosis 21:148 on 23 Oct 2026. It covers 8 randomized trials with 493 participants. Five trials enrolled people with type 2 diabetes. By drug: exenatide 5 trials, liraglutide 2, dulaglutide 1, semaglutide 1 (Hansen 2024, n=64). Tirzepatide is not included. The semaglutide trial found lower lumbar spine bone density (−0.018 g/cm² versus placebo). Certainty is very low for every drug. The authors call for adequately powered trials with fracture endpoints. Zibellini 2015 (J Bone Miner Res 30(12):2168–2178) found that diet-induced weight loss was linked to significant total-hip bone density drops of 0.010–0.015 g/cm², which supports "linked to a small hip bone density drop". The CDC adult page (last reviewed 20 Dec 2023) says muscle-strengthening on 2 or more days a week. The NHS semaglutide page lists feeling sick (nausea) as a common side effect. The framing is sound: no causal overreach, honest uncertainty, and nothing scary or falsely reassuring. The protein tip has a "clinician limits it" caveat for people with kidney conditions. Osteoporosis and fracture risk point to a clinician. The prescriber line, "Not personal advice" and the don't-stop/change line are all there. The CTA correctly says "Follow for more" because no related long-form is live. Narration is exactly 170 words, which is at the limit. The title is a question and the script answers it honestly. Two minor fixes are listed below; neither blocks shipping.

issues.claim: The one small semaglutide trial did see lower spine bone density
issues.problem: The narration doesn't give the comparator or the group size. The source's comparison was against placebo in 64 adults. Our craft rules require the comparator and the group size for every result. Without them the line reads as a bare finding.
issues.fix: Narration: "Certainty? Very low. The one semaglutide trial, sixty-four adults, saw lower spine density than placebo, but the authors say the evidence is too thin to tell how these drugs affect bone. Fracture trials are needed." (This cuts 2 words overall, keeping the Short at 168 words, within the 170 limit.) Myth_fact fact: "Very low certainty. 1 semaglutide trial (64 adults) saw lower spine density vs placebo; too thin to tell yet"

issues.claim: Most tested older drugs: exenatide, liraglutide, dulaglutide.
issues.problem: This is accurate: 7 of 8 trials used those drugs, 5 of them exenatide. One point is worth knowing but isn't required: the review also saw lower spine density with higher-dose liraglutide, so the result isn't unique to semaglutide. The script doesn't say it is unique, so this is not wrong. No change is needed to ship.
issues.fix: Optional, only if room allows: on-screen list item 1 → "Mostly exenatide (5), liraglutide (2), dulaglutide (1)". No narration change.
